subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If xʸ = e^(x−y), show that dy/dx = log x/(1 + log x)².

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.199, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Short Answer question 2. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section B question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The mathematics was checked independently before writing: y = x/(1 + log x) satisfies xʸ = e^(x−y) numerically, and dy/dx = log x/(1 + log x)² agrees with a central difference quotient at x = 2 (0.24178872) and x = 5 (0.23636343).

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you do to xʸ first, and what you do with y after that.

steps.label: Take logarithms of both sides
steps.margin_note: First mark. The mark is for the logarithm step itself. Write log(e^(x−y)) = x − y in one move — log and e are inverse functions, so the right side needs no further work.
lines: Take logarithms on both sides (log means logₑ throughout):

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are taken on both sides, giving y log x = x − y.
accept: take log on both sides
logarithm both sides so the power comes down
log x to the y becomes y log x and log of e to the x minus y is x minus y
rendu vaipula log teesukovali
start with logarithms because y is in the exponent
apply log so the index comes in front

steps.why: A variable index cannot be differentiated by the power rule or by the exponential rule on its own. Taking logarithms brings the index down as a multiplier, and both sides then become expressions the product and quotient rules can handle.
common_mistakes: Writing log(xʸ) as (log x)ʸ instead of y log x.
Leaving the right side as log(e^(x−y)) without simplifying it to x − y.
steps.memory_tip: When the unknown sits in the index, the first line is always "take logarithms". The same opening move works for y = xʸ and for every xˣ question in this chapter.

steps.label: Make y the subject
steps.margin_note: Second mark. This is where the bracket (1 + log x) first appears, and it is the same bracket that must be squared in the final answer.
lines: Collect the y terms on one side:

recall.must_convey: That the y terms are collected and factored to give y = x/(1 + log x).
accept: take y common and get y into one plus log x equals x
make y the subject
y equals x by one plus log x
y ni common teesi x by one plus log x ravali
shift the y from the right side and factor it out
write y explicitly in terms of x
heard_as: x by one plus log x

steps.why: Once y is written explicitly in terms of x, one use of the quotient rule finishes the question. Differentiating the relation implicitly also works, but it leaves y in the derivative and needs this same substitution afterwards, so making y the subject now is fewer steps.
common_mistakes: Writing y log x + y as y(log x) + y and failing to factor it as y(1 + log x).
Dividing by log x instead of by the whole bracket (1 + log x).
steps.memory_tip: The bracket (1 + log x) appears here for the first time and then again, squared, in the answer — one bracket carried through the whole question.

steps.label: Differentiate by the quotient rule
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Name u and v before differentiating. The examiner looks for dv/dx = 1/x — the derivative of the constant 1 is zero, so only log x contributes.
lines: Differentiate both sides with respect to x by the quotient rule
d/dx (u/v) = (v·du/dx − u·dv/dx)/v²,  with u = x and v = 1 + log x
dy/dx = [(1 + log x)(1) − x(1/x)]/(1 + log x)²

recall.must_convey: That the quotient rule is applied with u = x and v = 1 + log x, and that dv/dx = 1/x.
accept: apply the quotient rule with u equal to x and v equal to one plus log x
v du minus u dv all over v squared
derivative of one plus log x is one by x
quotient rule use cheyyali u equals x v equals one plus log x
differentiate the fraction using the quotient rule
bottom times derivative of top minus top times derivative of bottom

steps.why: The derivative of 1 + log x is 1/x, and the numerator x cancels that 1/x exactly. That cancellation is what produces the printed form, so the quotient rule has to be written out in full before any simplifying.
common_mistakes: Writing the numerator as u·dv/dx − v·du/dx, which reverses the sign of the answer.
steps.memory_tip: Order matters in the quotient rule: bottom times derivative of top comes FIRST, then subtract top times derivative of bottom.

steps.label: Simplify to the required form
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The denominator stays squared. A common loss is cancelling one factor of (1 + log x) between top and bottom, which is not allowed because log x is not a factor of (1 + log x).
lines: x(1/x) = 1, so the numerator is (1 + log x) − 1 = log x

recall.must_convey: That the numerator simplifies to log x and the answer is log x/(1 + log x)².
accept: the one cancels and only log x is left on top
answer is log x by one plus log x whole squared
numerator becomes log x, denominator stays squared
pina log x, kinda one plus log x square
x into one by x is one so the one goes
we reach exactly the required form

steps.why: The 1 inside the bracket cancels against the 1 produced by x(1/x), leaving log x alone in the numerator. Reaching exactly the printed expression is what a "show that" question asks for.
common_mistakes: Cancelling (1 + log x) between numerator and denominator.
Stopping at (1 + log x − 1)/(1 + log x)² without simplifying the numerator.
steps.memory_tip: Top loses its 1, bottom keeps its square — that one sentence is the whole simplification.

insider_note: Taking logarithms gives y log x = x − y, which SOLVES for y as x/(1 + log x). Differentiating that quotient is far easier than implicit differentiation of the original.
